figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Streaming implementation validation. A four-step checkpoint generates a real continuous 10-second HDTF chain with one persistent bounded cache, overlapping long-audio Whisper features, and streaming VAE state. The absolute cache endpoint reaches 65 latent frames while retained KV saturates at 22 (one reference plus 21 video frames). TTFF is 1.16s and peak allocated memory is 23.04GiB. Official SyncNet evaluation in two independent five-second windows gives Sync-C/D $10.086/6.407$ and $9.719/6.725$, with zero offset in both windows; thus the persistent cache has zero measured offset drift in this interface test. The later 60-second audit exposes lower-face collapse despite stable synchronization. The measured end-to-end system RTF is 5.97.
figures.headline: Streaming checkpoint keeps zero measured offset across two five-second windows, with Sync-C of 10.086 and 9.719.

abstract: Video dubbing aims to synthesize lip movements that match target speech while preserving the speaker identity, head pose, and background of a source video. Existing editors are predominantly trained via self-reconstruction under original paired audio, even though the source mouth becomes a conflicting target when driving speech is replaced. We introduce replacement-aware cross-audio supervision: paired-audio samples use full-frame reconstruction, whereas unpaired replacement-audio samples mask out source-mouth reconstruction losses and supervise the mouth solely through audio–visual synchronization while preserving unmasked facial regions and background. Because offline dubbing provides the complete source video and target speech beforehand, we present VidDub, a full-context diffusion editor distilled into two denoising steps (2 NFE). Our replacement-aware teacher first learns accurate lip synchronization without regressing toward conflicting source mouth movements. Matched trajectory regression then transfers the teacher’s CFG-guided trajectories to a two-step student, and distribution matching distillation recovers visual quality after step compression. We will release the curated training dataset, VidDub-Bench, fixed paired- and cross-audio evaluation manifests, preprocessing outputs, and unified evaluation code. Across three training seeds, masking out conflicting source-mouth reconstruction improves cross-audio Sync-C by $0.833\pm 0.040$; the final two-step model combines strong lip synchronization with superior visual quality, identity preservation, and visual speech recognition across four benchmarks.

sections.body: The paper argues that same-audio self-reconstruction training pulls generated lips toward the source mouth, which conflicts with dubbing under replacement speech. It proposes replacement-aware cross-audio supervision: paired clips use full-frame reconstruction, while unpaired replacement clips mask source-mouth losses and supervise the mouth only through audio–visual synchronization. The full-context teacher is distilled into a two-step (2 NFE) student through trajectory regression and distribution matching. The introduction reports a cross-audio Sync-C gain of +0.833±0.040 across three seeds and claims the best cross-audio synchronization among compared methods. It also contributes 85,435 curated training clips and the VidDub-Bench set of 256 videos.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Same-audio reconstruction training conflicts with replacement-speech dubbing, so the paper masks conflicting mouth losses and distills to two steps.

sections.body: This section groups prior work into visual speech editing, few-step video diffusion, and dubbing benchmarks. It states that standard self-reconstruction penalizes deviations from the source mouth, whereas the proposed objective masks source-mouth reconstruction on unpaired audio clips during training. For few-step diffusion, it notes that Causal Forcing and Lip Forcing combine causal attention with few-step distillation for online streaming, while offline dubbing provides the full source video and replacement audio beforehand. The method keeps full-window bidirectional attention and distills a guided teacher into a two-step student. For evaluation it adds SyncNet-based synchronization, an independent visual speech recognizer, identity similarity, head pose accuracy, Fréchet video distance (FVD), and 60-second temporal stability.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work contrasts same-audio reconstruction training and causal streaming with offline full-window two-step editing.

sections.body: Under replacement audio, the flow-matching loss uses the spatial weight $\bar{M}=1-M$, where $M$ is a latent mouth mask, so source-mouth velocity is not regressed. Pixel and perceptual mouth losses are dropped on those clips, and a preservation loss keeps non-mouth pixels. Lip sync is supervised by a frozen LatentSync-1.6 StableSyncNet loss. The generator is Wan-1.3B with video context conditioning and a 287M audio adapter over frozen Whisper-small features, with bidirectional self-attention over 21 video latents per 81-frame window. The two-step student shares the teacher architecture and reduces sampling from 48 steps to 2. Training runs teacher refinement with 70% paired and 30% replacement clips, guided trajectory regression, and distribution matching distillation (DMD).
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Source-mouth losses are masked under replacement audio, and a full-context teacher is distilled into a two-step student.

sections.body: Experiments use 81-frame, 24 FPS, 512×512 model calls on a 30-clip subset of a high-resolution talking-face set, TalkVid-Bench-500, and VidDub-Bench-256, with paired source-level bootstrap intervals. Table 4 shows replacement-aware teacher supervision raises cross-audio Sync-C on all four benchmarks, for example from 7.986 to 9.422 on HDTF-30. Table 5 reports that masking source-mouth reconstruction gives +0.833±0.040 Sync-C across three seeds, the largest factor, while audio dropout gives -0.019. On a 245-clip generated subset, the two-step student matches the teacher's cross-audio Sync-C. Table 7 gives the lowest independent visual-only word error rate among external methods on all three test sources. Table 10 reports Sync-C of 9.399 on 20 sixty-second pairs.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Masking conflicting mouth loss raises cross-audio Sync-C in ablations, and the final model has the lowest external visual-only word error rate.

sections.body: The conclusion restates two components: replacement-aware cross-audio supervision, which masks source-mouth reconstruction under unpaired replacement speech while keeping non-mouth reconstruction and synchronization, and full-context trajectory regression to two denoising steps followed by distribution matching. It states that across four source domains, VidDub combines accurate replacement-speech articulation with identity preservation and stable minute-long generation. The section reports no new numbers and adds no limitations beyond these claims.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion summarizes VidDub's two components and claims combined articulation accuracy, identity preservation, and stable minute-long output.

sections.body: The appendix gives data construction and split details, including 322,513 eligible teacher clips and zero source-video overlap between training, development, and VidDub-Bench. Table 12 compares a matched causal two-step variant with the full-context model: first output takes 1.052 s versus 7.165 s, while peak memory is 21.96 versus 13.77 GiB. The full-context model wins all six visual speech recognition comparisons, and the causal variant wins none. Further sections cover teacher training stages, streaming and long-video checks, a blinded human evaluation of 150 trials, qualitative case figures, and ethical safeguards.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists data splits, causal-variant comparisons, long-video and human-study tables, qualitative figures, and ethical safeguards.
